A1.justification: Both PDFs describe KernelCraft, with matching core tasks, framework and case studies. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the main text and appendices, including relocated material and rotated performance tables.

before.justification: v1 reports original kernel-generation success rates, measured performance, reasoning and in-context-learning ablations, CPU evaluations and compiler/ISA case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds SASS evaluation, correctness robustness tests, harness ablations, baseline comparisons and diagnostic analyses.

M1.justification: The native tool-calling generation-and-repair loop and correctness-first, performance-second workflow remain unchanged. The SASS extension applies this framework to another backend; alternative tolerance checks concern evaluation rather than a revised kernel-generation algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds NVIDIA SASS kernel generation across ten primitive workloads, extending coverage beyond the existing NPUs and BOOM CPU (Section 5.3, Table 15). It also introduces explicit input-distribution scenarios involving magnitude changes, boundary values and outliers (Table 13).

E2.justification: Table 27 newly evaluates KernelBench adapted to C++ without KernelCraft documentation/tools, and an iterative C++ agent supplied with KernelCraft prompts and documentation. These add direct pipeline comparisons beyond v1's model, compiler and human-expert comparisons; KernelBench previously appeared only in contextual comparisons and discussion.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled documentation/tool/prompt removals, alternative CUTLASS and Triton correctness checks, a 13-condition robustness protocol, and pass@k and instruction-coverage evaluations. Appendix C.1 also revises the stated AMD compilation path from direct PyTorch-to-Peano compilation to MLIR-AIR lowering followed by Peano, without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained reasoning and in-context-learning ablations, v2 adds documentation-density, individual-tool, prompt-component and supporting-file ablations (Tables 22–26). It also adds tolerance/input robustness tests, error breakdowns, tool-use analyses, configuration-scaling analyses and ISA-coverage analysis (Appendices C.2, F and G).

E5.justification: v2 first reports 95% confidence intervals for mean speedup in Figures 14–16 and explicitly tests five random input seeds in Table 13. v1 already reported five-configuration results and five-run averages. No increase in main-experiment generation repetitions is established, and the confidence-interval estimator is unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 5 changes GPT-5.2's PLENA RoPE result from 0/5 to 1/5 and its aggregate from 55/100 to 56/100. Substantial new results include SASS successes of 3/50 for GPT-5.2 and 0/50 for each other model, robustness and diagnostic results, and Table 27's success counts of 0/6 for KernelBench, 4/6 for the C++ agent and 5/6 for KernelCraft.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds explicit symmetric and near-zero acceptance inequalities for the newly evaluated CUTLASS check. Appendix G.4 defines instruction coverage through fractions of ISA instructions exercised and their union across workloads. These are limited mathematical specifications for evaluation; no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The introduction revises its headline success figure from 55% to 56%, accompanying the corrected PLENA aggregate. The central claims about benchmark novelty, autonomous assembly generation, hardware-aware optimization and compiler/ISA co-design remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of platform-specific prompt dependence, documentation and memory-layout importance, failure mechanisms, SASS difficulty, input robustness and benchmark coverage. Section 7 also removes v1's explicit explanation that tested-input correctness does not guarantee correctness across the input space and limits safety-critical applicability, retaining only a shorter numerical-validation caveat.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-access link, identifies CuAssembler-based SASS documentation preparation, explicitly names numpy.allclose, and corrects the AMD compiler-stack description. Existing model/API settings are relocated unchanged to Appendix C.4. Prompt excerpts receive small edits, including removal of two Coral memory-transfer guidance sentences.

R1.justification: CuAssembler is newly cited for the SASS extension. The separate AI CUDA Engineer bibliography entry is removed, while its discussion uses the remaining Lange citation. Appendix A otherwise retains the positioning against CUDA, Triton and compiler-IR approaches; most other reference changes concern metadata and formatting.

P1.justification: v2 streamlines the abstract and several explanatory passages, compresses future work, adds disclosure and conference front matter, corrects the token-analysis heading, and relocates model settings. New appendix sections reorganize supporting material, but the overall narrative and main section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with tolerance, robustness, SASS, harness-comparison and ISA-coverage tables, plus documentation, error, tool-use and scaling plots. Existing token-usage Figures 4–5 are consolidated onto one appendix page. The original architecture diagrams and principal result-table designs are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's limited harness validation with substantial ablations, robustness tests and competing pipelines. However, Table 22's PLENA D3 rows sum to 15/20 while its total and Figure 6 report 12/20. Appendix C.2 claims all alternative-tolerance checks pass although Table 12 reports match rates down to 97.3%. These inconsistencies affect important new validation claims, leaving the net quality benefit uncertain.
